voice_notes: Warm, measured adult narrator. 1880s newspaper editor reading a letter.
text:
A week has passed. Tomorrow, New York elects a mayor, and the Lower East Side is loud with it.

The Editor wants his front page by election night, or he finds another kid.

Go back to Hester Street. Find out what happened to Rivka's family, and what your choices have done.

voice_notes: Warm, measured adult narrator. 1880s newspaper editor reading a letter.
text:
The polls have closed. Thousands of New Yorkers pack Park Row, waiting for the returns to be posted outside the newspaper offices.

Find your friends in the crowd. Watch the results come in.

voice_notes: Warm, measured adult narrator. 1880s newspaper editor reading a letter.
text:
You are fifteen. Your mother and father landed at Castle Garden before you were born. A month ago the Evening Courier hired you to carry glass plates and sweep the darkroom.

Then the Editor put a camera in your hands.

"Thousands of newcomers land here every week, kid. Our readers argue about them and have never met one. Who are they? Why do they come? Is America what they were promised?"

He sent you across the ocean on a mail ship. You are coming home the hard way: in steerage, with a camera and $2.50.

"Bring me a front page and the job is yours. Come back with nothing, and I find another kid."

voice_notes: Warm, measured adult narrator. 1880s newspaper editor reading a letter.
text:
Day 12 at sea. Below deck, hundreds of passengers crowd into the hold.

Talk to the passengers. Find out what pushed them to leave home, and what pulled them to America. Use your camera to collect evidence.

voice_notes: Warm, measured adult narrator. 1880s newspaper editor reading a letter.
text:
The ship has landed. Before America, there is Castle Garden: an old fort that became New York's immigrant station. Since 1855, more than eight million people have passed through its doors.

Follow Rivka's family through inspection. Find out who gets in, and who does not.

voice_notes: Warm, measured adult narrator. 1880s newspaper editor reading a letter.
text:
Rivka's family has reached Hester Street, one of the most crowded neighborhoods on Earth.

Find Cousin Moishe's tenement. See how newcomers live, work, and help each other. Photograph what you find.

voice_notes: Warm, measured adult narrator. 1880s newspaper editor reading a letter.
text:
Election eve. Banners hang across Broadway, and the newspapers on Park Row are racing to print.

Giuseppe is waiting at the Times Building. Your editor wants to see you at the Courier office before tonight's deadline.

voice_notes: Girl, about 16. Jewish, from near Kiev. Light Yiddish/Russian accent. Brave but tired.
text: You are the one with the camera box? Mama says not to stare. But everyone stares at it.

voice_notes: Girl, about 16. Jewish, from near Kiev. Light Yiddish/Russian accent. Brave but tired.
text: You are no older than me. And a newspaper sends you across the ocean alone?

voice_notes: Girl, about 16. Jewish, from near Kiev. Light Yiddish/Russian accent. Brave but tired.
text: In 1881, someone killed the Tsar. People blamed the Jews.

voice_notes: Girl, about 16. Jewish, from near Kiev. Light Yiddish/Russian accent. Brave but tired.
text: Mobs attacked Jewish towns. These attacks are called pogrom.

voice_notes: Girl, about 16. Jewish, from near Kiev. Light Yiddish/Russian accent. Brave but tired.
text: They smashed our windows. They burned Papa's shop. The police watched and did nothing.

voice_notes: Girl, about 16. Jewish, from near Kiev. Light Yiddish/Russian accent. Brave but tired.
text: Then came new rules, the May Laws. Jews could not move to new villages. We could not buy land.

voice_notes: Girl, about 16. Jewish, from near Kiev. Light Yiddish/Russian accent. Brave but tired.
text: Papa died the next winter. Mama said, "There is no future for us here."

voice_notes: Girl, about 16. Jewish, from near Kiev. Light Yiddish/Russian accent. Brave but tired.
text: Moishe's letter! I read it every night. Here, you may look.

voice_notes: Girl, about 16. Jewish, from near Kiev. Light Yiddish/Russian accent. Brave but tired.
text: Without this address, we would know no one in America.

voice_notes: Girl, about 16. Jewish, from near Kiev. Light Yiddish/Russian accent. Brave but tired.
text: With it, we have family waiting. Moishe came first. Now we follow. Maybe someday we send for others.

voice_notes: Girl, about 16. Jewish, from near Kiev. Light Yiddish/Russian accent. Brave but tired.
text: A picture? Of us? ...Yes. Please.

voice_notes: Girl, about 16. Jewish, from near Kiev. Light Yiddish/Russian accent. Brave but tired.
text: My Bubbe, my grandmother, stayed behind. She is too old for the ship. She cried so hard at the station, the conductor waited.

voice_notes: Girl, about 16. Jewish, from near Kiev. Light Yiddish/Russian accent. Brave but tired.
text: If you send her a picture, she will know we are alive. That we made it.

voice_notes: Warm, measured adult narrator. 1880s newspaper editor reading a letter.
text: You promise Rivka a print. (Press F to raise your camera, then aim at her.)

voice_notes: Woman, 40s, Yiddish accent, worried and gentle.
text: Rivka does the talking. Her English is better than mine.

voice_notes: Woman, 40s, Yiddish accent, worried and gentle.
text: Shmuel coughs at night. Since Hamburg. If the American doctors hear it, they send him back.

voice_notes: Woman, 40s, Yiddish accent, worried and gentle.
text: Back to what? There is nothing to go back to. Please. Do not tell anyone.

voice_notes: Boy, about 8.
text: Is it true the streets in America are made of gold?

voice_notes: Boy, about 8.
text: Mr. Novak is making me a horse! Out of wood! He says it can swim across the ocean.

voice_notes: Warm, measured adult narrator. 1880s newspaper editor reading a letter.
text: Shmuel coughs, a deep rattling cough. He looks at his mother, frightened, and covers his mouth.

voice_notes: Man, 20s, southern Italian accent, cheerful and proud, a little homesick.
text: Ah, a photographer! Here, catch!

voice_notes: Warm, measured adult narrator. 1880s newspaper editor reading a letter.
text: He tosses you a lemon, wrinkled from twelve days at sea.

voice_notes: Man, 20s, southern Italian accent, cheerful and proud, a little homesick.
text: From my mother's tree. Smell it. That is Calabria. That is home.

voice_notes: Man, 20s, southern Italian accent, cheerful and proud, a little homesick.
text: Keep it! Take my picture instead. Make me look rich, so Mamma is proud.

voice_notes: Man, 20s, southern Italian accent, cheerful and proud, a little homesick.
text: Photographer! You still have my lemon? Good. Don't eat it. It's not for eating. It's for remembering.

voice_notes: Man, 20s, southern Italian accent, cheerful and proud, a little homesick.
text: The land belongs to rich landlords. We work it. They keep most of the crops.

voice_notes: Man, 20s, southern Italian accent, cheerful and proud, a little homesick.
text: Every year, the taxes go up. The soil is tired. A man works all day, and still his children are hungry.

voice_notes: Man, 20s, southern Italian accent, cheerful and proud, a little homesick.
text: America needs strong backs! They are building railroads, streets, buildings, everything.

voice_notes: Man, 20s, southern Italian accent, cheerful and proud, a little homesick.
text: My cousin says a man can earn a dollar a day digging. At home, I am lucky to earn twenty cents.

voice_notes: Man, 20s, southern Italian accent, cheerful and proud, a little homesick.
text: I will work three, four years. Save every penny. Go home, buy land of my own.

voice_notes: Man, 20s, southern Italian accent, cheerful and proud, a little homesick.
text: Many of us do this. The Americans call us bird of passage.

voice_notes: Man, 20s, southern Italian accent, cheerful and proud, a little homesick.
text: A man in Naples, a padrone, promised me a job is waiting. He takes a little of my pay. My cousin says, "Be careful. Some padrones are thieves."

voice_notes: Man, 50s, German accent, slow and serious, a bit stubborn.
text: Guten Tag. You are American? Good. Then tell me: is the soil in Wisconsin as rich as they say?

voice_notes: Man, 50s, German accent, slow and serious, a bit stubborn.
text: In Pomerania, we rent a small farm. Now cheap grain comes from America and Russia, and our prices fall and fall.

voice_notes: Man, 50s, German accent, slow and serious, a bit stubborn.
text: Also, my son would have to serve years in the army. I would rather he plow a field in Wisconsin.

voice_notes: Man, 50s, German accent, slow and serious, a bit stubborn.
text: Ja. We Germans, the Irish, the English, we have come to America for fifty years. People call us the old immigrants.

voice_notes: Man, 50s, German accent, slow and serious, a bit stubborn.
text: But now look: Italians. Russian Jews. Poles. Greeks. So many new immigrants. Different churches, different food. I do not know their ways.

voice_notes: Man, 50s, German accent, slow and serious, a bit stubborn.
text: When my grandfather's cousins came to America, people asked the same question about Germans. I suppose every ship asks it.

voice_notes: Woman, 50s, German accent.
text: Twelve days at sea, and the bread is already green.

voice_notes: Woman, 50s, German accent.
text: Do not write that in your newspaper. Well... perhaps you should.

voice_notes: Elderly man, 70s, Czech/Bohemian accent, quiet and dignified.
text: Sit, sit. My hands need work, or they forget.

voice_notes: Warm, measured adult narrator. 1880s newspaper editor reading a letter.
text: The old man is carving a little wooden horse with a pocketknife. Curls of wood collect in his lap.

voice_notes: Elderly man, 70s, Czech/Bohemian accent, quiet and dignified.
text: For the boy with the cough. Every child should own a horse.

voice_notes: Elderly man, 70s, Czech/Bohemian accent, quiet and dignified.
text: My son Tomas went to Chicago eleven years ago. He writes every Christmas.

voice_notes: Elderly man, 70s, Czech/Bohemian accent, quiet and dignified.
text: My wife died in the spring. So I sold the loom, the house, everything, for the ticket.

voice_notes: Elderly man, 70s, Czech/Bohemian accent, quiet and dignified.
text: Tomas does not know I am coming. I will knock on his door. A surprise!

voice_notes: Elderly man, 70s, Czech/Bohemian accent, quiet and dignified.
text: Wrong? I am seventy-two. Everything already went wrong once. Then you start again.

voice_notes: Man, 40s, Welsh/English sailor, gruff, matter-of-fact.
text: Mind your head. Low beams down here, and lower tempers.

voice_notes: Man, 40s, Welsh/English sailor, gruff, matter-of-fact.
text: steerage. Cheapest ticket on the ship. Near a thousand souls below decks on this crossing.

voice_notes: Man, 40s, Welsh/English sailor, gruff, matter-of-fact.
text: Iron berths, two high, six feet by two. A sack of straw, one blanket, and a cork life preserver for a pillow.

voice_notes: Man, 40s, Welsh/English sailor, gruff, matter-of-fact.
text: Single men sleep forward, single women aft, and families here in the middle.

voice_notes: Man, 40s, Welsh/English sailor, gruff, matter-of-fact.
text: Upstairs, first class has a dining room with chandeliers. Same ship. Different world.

voice_notes: Man, 40s, Welsh/English sailor, gruff, matter-of-fact.
text: Tomorrow morning, if the fog lifts. When you're ready, climb the ladder up through the hatch.

voice_notes: Man, 50s, American, brisk and official.
text: Next! Step forward. Look at me. Open your eyes wide.

voice_notes: Man, 50s, American, brisk and official.
text: You'll do. Move along. Next!

voice_notes: Warm, measured adult narrator. 1880s newspaper editor reading a letter.
text: The doctor turns to Shmuel. The boy coughs. Mrs. Abramowitz grips your arm so hard it hurts.

voice_notes: Man, 50s, American, brisk and official.
text: This one. Open your mouth. Breathe. Again. ...Again.

voice_notes: Warm, measured adult narrator. 1880s newspaper editor reading a letter.
text: The whole line has gone quiet.

voice_notes: Man, 50s, American, brisk and official.
text: ...Seasick. Half the ship is seasick. Move along.

voice_notes: Woman, 40s, Yiddish accent, worried and gentle.
text: Thank God. Thank God.

voice_notes: Man, 50s, American, brisk and official.
text: Contagious disease: fever, smallpox, bad coughs. And anyone too sick or weak to work and support themselves.

voice_notes: Man, 50s, American, brisk and official.
text: If it's catching, they go to the hospital on Ward's Island.

voice_notes: Man, 50s, American, brisk and official.
text: If we turn them away, the steamship company must carry them home, at the company's own cost.

voice_notes: Man, 30s, New York accent, tired, fast-talking but not unkind.
text: Next! Family of three? All right, miss, you're translating?

voice_notes: Girl, about 16. Jewish, from near Kiev. Light Yiddish/Russian accent. Brave but tired.
text: Yes, sir.

voice_notes: Man, 30s, New York accent, tired, fast-talking but not unkind.
text: Name, country, job, and where you're going.

voice_notes: Girl, about 16. Jewish, from near Kiev. Light Yiddish/Russian accent. Brave but tired.
text: Rivka Abramowitz. Russia. I sew. We go to Hester Street, New York.

voice_notes: Man, 30s, New York accent, tired, fast-talking but not unkind.
text: Do you have money? Is anyone meeting you?

voice_notes: Girl, about 16. Jewish, from near Kiev. Light Yiddish/Russian accent. Brave but tired.
text: Our cousin, Moishe Abramowitz. He is a tailor. Here is his address.

voice_notes: Man, 30s, New York accent, tired, fast-talking but not unkind.
text: Family with a job and an address. Good. That's what I like to see. Next!

voice_notes: Man, 30s, New York accent, tired, fast-talking but not unkind.
text: Convicts. People who are insane. And anyone "public charge."

voice_notes: Man, 30s, New York accent, tired, fast-talking but not unkind.
text: That means anybody we think will end up living off charity. Old folks alone. No money, no family, no work.

voice_notes: Man, 30s, New York accent, tired, fast-talking but not unkind.
text: Family waiting means somebody will feed you while you find work. To me, that address is worth more than gold.

voice_notes: Elderly man, 70s, Czech/Bohemian accent, quiet and dignified.
text: Photographer! You remember me, from the ship?

voice_notes: Elderly man, 70s, Czech/Bohemian accent, quiet and dignified.
text: They keep me here, on this bench. "Public charge," they say. Old, no money, nobody meeting me.

voice_notes: Elderly man, 70s, Czech/Bohemian accent, quiet and dignified.
text: I tell them, my son Tomas is in Chicago! They say, "Then where is he?"

voice_notes: Elderly man, 70s, Czech/Bohemian accent, quiet and dignified.
text: A telegram to Chicago costs twenty-five cents. I have four cents. Everything else went for the ticket.

voice_notes: Elderly man, 70s, Czech/Bohemian accent, quiet and dignified.
text: If no one comes for me in three days, they put me back on the ship.

voice_notes: Warm, measured adult narrator. 1880s newspaper editor reading a letter.
text: You count out the coins. Mr. Novak holds them a long time before he closes his hand.

voice_notes: Elderly man, 70s, Czech/Bohemian accent, quiet and dignified.
text: Tomas Novak. Halsted Street, Chicago. "Your father is at Castle Garden. Come."

voice_notes: Elderly man, 70s, Czech/Bohemian accent, quiet and dignified.
text: If he comes, I owe you my life. If he does not... I owe you anyway.

voice_notes: Elderly man, 70s, Czech/Bohemian accent, quiet and dignified.
text: No, no. You are young. Your money is your future. I understand.

voice_notes: Warm, measured adult narrator. 1880s newspaper editor reading a letter.
text: He goes back to carving. The little horse for Shmuel is almost finished.

voice_notes: Elderly man, 70s, Czech/Bohemian accent, quiet and dignified.
text: Every time the door opens, I think: Tomas. Not yet. Not yet.

voice_notes: Elderly man, 70s, Czech/Bohemian accent, quiet and dignified.
text: The horse is finished. Give it to the boy for me, if I cannot.

voice_notes: Girl, about 16. Jewish, from near Kiev. Light Yiddish/Russian accent. Brave but tired.
text: So many men shouting! Everyone wants our bags, our money...

voice_notes: Girl, about 16. Jewish, from near Kiev. Light Yiddish/Russian accent. Brave but tired.
text: Mama is frightened. You know this city better than we do. Who should we trust?

voice_notes: Girl, about 16. Jewish, from near Kiev. Light Yiddish/Russian accent. Brave but tired.
text: All right. But hurry, please. Shmuel is hungry.

voice_notes: Warm, measured adult narrator. 1880s newspaper editor reading a letter.
text: Jack grabs the bags and leads them to a crowded boardinghouse on Greenwich Street.

voice_notes: Warm, measured adult narrator. 1880s newspaper editor reading a letter.
text: There, the "one dollar" bed suddenly costs five. Jack will not return the bags until they pay.

voice_notes: Girl, about 16. Jewish, from near Kiev. Light Yiddish/Russian accent. Brave but tired.
text: He lied to us! Almost half our money is gone. How will we start?

voice_notes: Warm, measured adult narrator. 1880s newspaper editor reading a letter.
text: You help them get away and find the way to Hester Street. Runners like Jack cheated thousands of newcomers.

voice_notes: Warm, measured adult narrator. 1880s newspaper editor reading a letter.
text: The money changer counts quickly and hands over a small pile of American coins.

voice_notes: Girl, about 16. Jewish, from near Kiev. Light Yiddish/Russian accent. Brave but tired.
text: Wait. This is much less than the sign inside said! He cheated us!

voice_notes: Warm, measured adult narrator. 1880s newspaper editor reading a letter.
text: He has already vanished into the crowd. Rivka's family has lost a good part of their savings.

voice_notes: Warm, measured adult narrator. 1880s newspaper editor reading a letter.
text: Miss Carver changes their money at the official rate and draws a map to Hester Street.

voice_notes: Girl, about 16. Jewish, from near Kiev. Light Yiddish/Russian accent. Brave but tired.
text: She says Moishe lives only a few miles away. We can walk! Thank you, thank you.

voice_notes: Girl, about 16. Jewish, from near Kiev. Light Yiddish/Russian accent. Brave but tired.
text: My heart is pounding. What if they send us back? Where would we even go?

voice_notes: Girl, about 16. Jewish, from near Kiev. Light Yiddish/Russian accent. Brave but tired.
text: Stay close to us, please. Go see the doctor first. Then the clerk will call us.

voice_notes: Man, 30s, fast, overly friendly New York hustler.
text: Welcome to America, friends! Welcome, welcome!

voice_notes: Man, 30s, fast, overly friendly New York hustler.
text: Best boardinghouse in New York! Clean beds, hot meals, only one dollar! Here, give me your bags. I'll carry them for you!

voice_notes: Man, 30s, fast, overly friendly New York hustler.
text: Me? I just love helping newcomers! That's all! Ha ha. Now, those bags...

voice_notes: Man, 40s, slick, smooth-talking.
text: Rubles? Lire? Marks? I change them all! Best rate in New York!

voice_notes: Man, 40s, slick, smooth-talking.
text: Inside, they make you wait in line. With me? Quick, quick. Nobody waits.

voice_notes: Woman, 30s, American, patient and clear.
text: Information desk. How can I help?

voice_notes: Woman, 30s, American, patient and clear.
text: Whatever you do, don't hand your bags to strangers outside that gate. And change your money only at the official counter.

voice_notes: Woman, 30s, American, patient and clear.
text: If you have an address, show it to me. I'll tell you how to get there.

voice_notes: Woman, 30s, American, patient and clear.
text: Runners. They're paid by boardinghouses, ticket sellers, and worse. Some are honest. Most are not.

voice_notes: Woman, 30s, American, patient and clear.
text: They speak your language, smile, and promise everything. That's how they get you.

voice_notes: Girl, about 16. Jewish, from near Kiev. Light Yiddish/Russian accent. Brave but tired.
text: This is it! Hester Street. The number matches the letter!

voice_notes: Girl, about 16. Jewish, from near Kiev. Light Yiddish/Russian accent. Brave but tired.
text: Moishe lives inside, on the ground floor. Come, come in with us!

voice_notes: Girl, about 16. Jewish, from near Kiev. Light Yiddish/Russian accent. Brave but tired.
text: Two rooms. Nine people. And it is ours.

voice_notes: Girl, about 16. Jewish, from near Kiev. Light Yiddish/Russian accent. Brave but tired.
text: Tomorrow Moishe takes me to a shop that needs a girl for buttonholes. Tomorrow I start.

voice_notes: Man, 30s, Yiddish accent, kind, overworked, coughs a little.
text: Rivka! Mama! Shmuel! You are here! ...What? A runner took your money?

voice_notes: Man, 30s, Yiddish accent, kind, overworked, coughs a little.
text: Ach. They wait like wolves at Castle Garden. Don't worry. The Kiever Society will help. We help each other here.

voice_notes: Man, 30s, Yiddish accent, kind, overworked, coughs a little.
text: Rivka! Mama! You came! ...Cheated by a money changer? It happens to half of us.

voice_notes: Man, 30s, Yiddish accent, kind, overworked, coughs a little.
text: Don't cry. The Kiever Society will help. We help each other here.

voice_notes: Man, 30s, Yiddish accent, kind, overworked, coughs a little.
text: Rivka! Mama! Shmuel! You found me! The letter worked!

voice_notes: Man, 30s, Yiddish accent, kind, overworked, coughs a little.
text: And you, the photographer who helped them. Come in, come in. Mind the stairs. It's dark.

voice_notes: Man, 30s, Yiddish accent, kind, overworked, coughs a little.
text: I am a tailor. We sew coats, right here in the apartment.

voice_notes: Man, 30s, Yiddish accent, kind, overworked, coughs a little.
text: A contractor brings cut cloth in the morning. We sew. He pays by the coat. This is called piecework.

voice_notes: Man, 30s, Yiddish accent, kind, overworked, coughs a little.
text: If we sew fast, we eat. If we are slow, we don't. Fourteen hours a day, six days a week.

voice_notes: Man, 30s, Yiddish accent, kind, overworked, coughs a little.
text: Uptown people call a place like this a sweatshop. To me, it is home.

voice_notes: Man, 30s, Yiddish accent, kind, overworked, coughs a little.
text: ...Photograph the room. Photograph the machine. Photograph me, I don't care.

voice_notes: Man, 30s, Yiddish accent, kind, overworked, coughs a little.
text: But please. Not my Sarah's face.

voice_notes: Man, 30s, Yiddish accent, kind, overworked, coughs a little.
text: Mr. Kessler reads the newspapers. If he sees a child working in his coats, he says we make trouble, and the work goes to the next family. There is always a next family.

voice_notes: Man, 30s, Yiddish accent, kind, overworked, coughs a little.
text: Promise me you will think about it, before you print anything.

voice_notes: Man, 40s, Yiddish-German accent, brusque and defensive, tired; not a cartoon villain.
text: Ten coats. Eleven. Twelve. This one, the seam is crooked. Ten cents off.

voice_notes: Woman, 30s, Yiddish accent, practical and quick.
text: It is straight! Look at it! It is straight!

voice_notes: Man, 40s, Yiddish-German accent, brusque and defensive, tired; not a cartoon villain.
text: Then next week it is straight. This week, ten cents off.

voice_notes: Man, 40s, Yiddish-German accent, brusque and defensive, tired; not a cartoon villain.
text: You want the work, Mrs. Abramowitz, or should I give it to the Rosenbergs upstairs?

voice_notes: Warm, measured adult narrator. 1880s newspaper editor reading a letter.
text: Chana says nothing. Her hands are shaking.

voice_notes: Warm, measured adult narrator. 1880s newspaper editor reading a letter.
text: The shutter clicks. You have him, coins in his hand, Chana looking at the floor.

voice_notes: Man, 40s, Yiddish-German accent, brusque and defensive, tired; not a cartoon villain.
text: Put that thing away! You print my face, boy, and this family sews no more coats for me. You understand?

voice_notes: Warm, measured adult narrator. 1880s newspaper editor reading a letter.
text: You have the picture. Chana is still out her ten cents.

voice_notes: Man, 40s, Yiddish-German accent, brusque and defensive, tired; not a cartoon villain.
text: You are the newspaper's boy? Listen, kid.

voice_notes: Man, 40s, Yiddish-German accent, brusque and defensive, tired; not a cartoon villain.
text: The manufacturer on Broadway pays me less every season. If I don't squeeze, I lose the contract, and nobody in this building eats.

voice_notes: Man, 40s, Yiddish-German accent, brusque and defensive, tired; not a cartoon villain.
text: You want a villain for your newspaper? Go photograph the man on Broadway.

voice_notes: Warm, measured adult narrator. 1880s newspaper editor reading a letter.
text: He slaps Chana's ten cents down on the table and goes. You have no picture of any of it.

voice_notes: Man, 40s, Yiddish-German accent, brusque and defensive, tired; not a cartoon villain.
text: Good. A man who knows when to keep quiet. Next Friday, Moishe. Fourteen coats.

voice_notes: Woman, 30s, Yiddish accent, practical and quick.
text: Hand me that thread. No, the black one. Thank you.

voice_notes: Woman, 30s, Yiddish accent, practical and quick.
text: I am a finisher. Moishe sews the seams. I do buttonholes, hems, linings. A few pennies for each coat.

voice_notes: Woman, 30s, Yiddish accent, practical and quick.
text: In winter, we sew by the lamp until our eyes burn. In summer, it's so hot the cloth sticks to our hands.

voice_notes: Girl, about 10, Yiddish accent, shy.
text: I sew buttons after school. Mama says school comes first.

voice_notes: Girl, about 10, Yiddish accent, shy.
text: But buttons pay, so I sew fast. Look, twelve already!

voice_notes: Young man, 20, Yiddish accent, sleepy.
text: Shh. I work nights at the bakery. These two chairs? This is my bed.

voice_notes: Young man, 20, Yiddish accent, sleepy.
text: I pay Moishe a dollar a week. It's a bed and a roof. In America, that's a start.

voice_notes: Man, about 40, Danish accent, energetic, passionate about reform.
text: Ah! Another camera! Jacob Riis, police reporter, New York Tribune.

voice_notes: Man, about 40, Danish accent, energetic, passionate about reform.
text: I came from Denmark myself, in 1870. I slept in police station lodging rooms, hungry. I know these streets.

voice_notes: Man, about 40, Danish accent, energetic, passionate about reform.
text: Agree? Ha. Most of them were asleep when the flash went off. Some ran. Some threw things.

voice_notes: Man, about 40, Danish accent, energetic, passionate about reform.
text: It frightens them, I know. But the city must see.

voice_notes: Warm, measured adult narrator. 1880s newspaper editor reading a letter.
text: You wonder: is it fair to photograph people without asking? Riis's pictures helped change laws, but some of what he wrote about immigrant groups was unkind and unfair.

voice_notes: Man, about 40, Danish accent, energetic, passionate about reform.
text: He is afraid. I understand. I have seen what bosses do.

voice_notes: Man, about 40, Danish accent, energetic, passionate about reform.
text: But hear me. Uptown, a picture of a dark room is just a dark room. Readers turn the page.

voice_notes: Man, about 40, Danish accent, energetic, passionate about reform.
text: A child's face at a sewing machine? That, nobody forgets. Faces change laws.

voice_notes: Man, about 40, Danish accent, energetic, passionate about reform.
text: And sometimes faces cost a family its work. That is the hard part of this job, friend. You will have to choose.

voice_notes: Woman, 40s, Yiddish accent, loud, funny, sharp businesswoman.
text: Pickles! Herring! Fresh onions! Cheaper than anywhere! You want? No? Then why are you standing in front of my cart?

voice_notes: Woman, 40s, Yiddish accent, loud, funny, sharp businesswoman.
text: A pushcart rents for ten cents a day. I buy at the market at dawn. I sell until dark. The profit is mine!

voice_notes: Woman, 40s, Yiddish accent, loud, funny, sharp businesswoman.
text: No boss yelling at me. No contractor. Just me, my cart, and my big mouth.

voice_notes: Woman, 40s, Yiddish accent, loud, funny, sharp businesswoman.
text: Someday, a store. With a sign! "Gold's." Why not?

voice_notes: Woman, 40s, Yiddish accent, loud, funny, sharp businesswoman.
text: One cent! The best pickle on Hester Street. Don't tell Herschel I said so. He thinks his are better.

voice_notes: Man, 50s, Yiddish accent.
text: Pots! Pans! Tin cups! In the old country, I was a teacher.

voice_notes: Man, 50s, Yiddish accent.
text: Here, I sell pots. My English is not good enough to teach. But my son? My son will be the teacher.

voice_notes: Boy, about 11, New York street accent, fast.
text: Extra, extra! Papers in every language! Two cents!

voice_notes: Boy, about 11, New York street accent, fast.
text: Yiddish paper! Italian paper! The German Staats-Zeitung! The Irish World! What'll it be, pal?

voice_notes: Boy, about 11, New York street accent, fast.
text: People want news from home! And they can't read English yet. Not good enough, anyway.

voice_notes: Boy, about 11, New York street accent, fast.
text: Look at the back pages: jobs, rooms for rent, lawyers, steamship tickets. Everything a greenhorn needs.

voice_notes: Boy, about 11, New York street accent, fast.
text: These ethnic newspaper tell you how to be an American, in your own language. Funny, huh?

voice_notes: Boy, about 11, New York street accent, fast.
text: Two cents! Thanks, pal! Read the back pages, that's where the jobs are.

voice_notes: Man, 60s, Yiddish accent, warm and formal.
text: Welcome to the new synagogue on Eldridge Street, finished just last year. I am Kaplan, secretary of the Kiever Society.

voice_notes: Man, 60s, Yiddish accent, warm and formal.
text: We are a landsmanshaft: everyone from Kiev and the towns nearby.

voice_notes: Man, 60s, Yiddish accent, warm and formal.
text: Each member pays a little every month. When someone is sick, we pay. When someone dies, we bury them properly.

voice_notes: Man, 60s, Yiddish accent, warm and formal.
text: When a newcomer arrives, we help find a room and a job.

voice_notes: Man, 60s, Yiddish accent, warm and formal.
text: The government? The government does not pay sick money. Charities make you beg.

voice_notes: Man, 60s, Yiddish accent, warm and formal.
text: So we do it for each other. That is mutual aid. The synagogue, the society, the Italian church, the Irish clubs. Everyone has something.

voice_notes: Man, 60s, Yiddish accent, warm and formal.
text: Bring them to me. The society will lend them enough to start. They will pay back when they can. That is what we are for.

voice_notes: Man, 50s, Italian accent, gentle.
text: Good day. This is the Church of the Transfiguration, on Mott Street. Protestants built it long ago, and the Irish made it a Catholic parish.

voice_notes: Man, 50s, Italian accent, gentle.
text: Now the Italians come too, and Chinese neighbors live all around us.

voice_notes: Man, 50s, Italian accent, gentle.
text: The Irish are not always happy to share their pews. Different saints, different songs.

voice_notes: Man, 50s, Italian accent, gentle.
text: But we run a school. We visit the sick. We help men find work. A parish is like a village inside the city.

voice_notes: Man, 20s, southern Italian accent, cheerful and proud, a little homesick.
text: Photographer! You made it too! Look at me, an American worker!

voice_notes: Man, 20s, southern Italian accent, cheerful and proud, a little homesick.
text: I live on Mulberry Street with men from my village. Eight of us in one room. We cook together, we send money home together.

voice_notes: Man, 20s, southern Italian accent, cheerful and proud, a little homesick.
text: I dig for a new street. A dollar a day... minus what the padrone takes. Still, it's more than Calabria.

voice_notes: Man, 40s, Cantonese accent, calm, careful, a little guarded.
text: Welcome to my shop. Tea, dried fish, rice, medicine. Letters from home. You want something?

voice_notes: Man, 40s, Cantonese accent, calm, careful, a little guarded.
text: White-owned businesses would not hire me. Not in a factory, not in a store.

voice_notes: Man, 40s, Cantonese accent, calm, careful, a little guarded.
text: So I work for myself. And I hire other Chinese. On Mott Street, we have our own shops, our own societies, our own help.

voice_notes: Man, 40s, Cantonese accent, calm, careful, a little guarded.
text: Yes. The Chinese Exclusion Act. Since 1882, no more Chinese laborers may come to America.

voice_notes: Man, 40s, Cantonese accent, calm, careful, a little guarded.
text: Because I am a merchant, I may stay. But I can never become a citizen. The law says so.

voice_notes: Man, 40s, Cantonese accent, calm, careful, a little guarded.
text: My brother is a laborer. He cannot come. I have not seen him in twenty years.

voice_notes: Man, 40s, Cantonese accent, calm, careful, a little guarded.
text: The Irish, the Germans, the Jews, they can all become citizens. Only us, the law shuts out by name.

voice_notes: Woman, 50s, Irish accent, sharp-tongued, proud, defensive.
text: Would you look at this street! Pushcarts, foreign talk, garlic. It's not the neighborhood I knew.

voice_notes: Woman, 50s, Irish accent, sharp-tongued, proud, defensive.
text: These new people come by the boatload. They work for nothing, and then decent folks can't get a fair wage.

voice_notes: Woman, 50s, Irish accent, sharp-tongued, proud, defensive.
text: My parents came from Ireland in '49, during the Famine. Half the village starved. We came with nothing.

voice_notes: Woman, 50s, Irish accent, sharp-tongued, proud, defensive.
text: We worked hard! We built this city.

voice_notes: Woman, 50s, Irish accent, sharp-tongued, proud, defensive.
text: Welcomed? Ha! Some job ads said "No Irish need apply." They called us dirty, and drunk, and said the Pope would rule America.

voice_notes: Woman, 50s, Irish accent, sharp-tongued, proud, defensive.
text: ...Well. That was different. We spoke English, at least.

voice_notes: Woman, 50s, Irish accent, sharp-tongued, proud, defensive.
text: ...Maybe they did say the same things. Maybe they do. I don't have to like it.

voice_notes: Young man, 20s, educated American, earnest.
text: Hello! Welcome to the Neighborhood Guild, here at 146 Forsyth Street. Dr. Stanton Coit started it in 1886. It's the first settlement house in America.

voice_notes: Young man, 20s, educated American, earnest.
text: We don't just visit the neighborhood. We live here. We run boys' and girls' clubs, a reading room, English classes, a kindergarten.

voice_notes: Young man, 20s, educated American, earnest.
text: You can't help people you don't know. Some people want to "fix" the immigrants.

voice_notes: Young man, 20s, educated American, earnest.
text: I think we should listen first. Mrs. Gold down the street knows more about business than any banker I've met.

voice_notes: Man, 40s, Irish-New York accent, booming and friendly. Fictional Tammany ward boss.
text: Cold night coming! Here, take a sack of coal for your family. No charge!

voice_notes: Man, 40s, Irish-New York accent, booming and friendly. Fictional Tammany ward boss.
text: Just remember who your friends are on Election Day. Ha ha!

voice_notes: Man, 40s, Irish-New York accent, booming and friendly. Fictional Tammany ward boss.
text: Me? Just a friend of the neighborhood. Ask anybody for Quinn, from the Tammany club on the corner.

voice_notes: Man, 40s, Irish-New York accent, booming and friendly. Fictional Tammany ward boss.
text: Because folks need it! And folks who get help... well, they remember. That's all. Next! Who needs coal?

voice_notes: Man, 60s, American, dry humor, a bit cynical.
text: You're the one doing the immigrant story? Haskins. Thirty years on Park Row. Come look at this.

voice_notes: Man, 60s, American, dry humor, a bit cynical.
text: William Magear Tweed. "Boss" Tweed. He ran Tammany Hall, the Democratic political club, in the 1860s.

voice_notes: Man, 60s, American, dry humor, a bit cynical.
text: Tammany ran the city like a machine: jobs, contracts, favors, votes. And Tweed's Ring stole from the city treasury. Tens of millions of dollars.

voice_notes: Man, 60s, American, dry humor, a bit cynical.
text: See that courthouse behind City Hall? It should have cost a few hundred thousand. They billed the city millions. One plasterer was paid over a hundred thousand dollars for two days' work!

voice_notes: Man, 60s, American, dry humor, a bit cynical.
text: Gone? Ha! Tweed is gone. Tammany got smarter.

voice_notes: Man, 60s, American, dry humor, a bit cynical.
text: Go talk to Plunkitt. He sits at the bootblack stand inside the courthouse, of all places. He'll tell you how it works. He loves to talk.

voice_notes: Man, mid-40s, Irish-New York accent, folksy, proud, chuckles at his own jokes.
text: Sit down, young fella! Get a shine! This here bootblack stand is my office.

voice_notes: Man, mid-40s, Irish-New York accent, folksy, proud, chuckles at his own jokes.
text: George Washington Plunkitt, Tammany leader of the Fifteenth District. What can I do for you?

voice_notes: Man, mid-40s, Irish-New York accent, folksy, proud, chuckles at his own jokes.
text: Easy! We help people. A family is burned out of their home at two in the morning? I'm there before the fire engines leave.

voice_notes: Man, mid-40s, Irish-New York accent, folksy, proud, chuckles at his own jokes.
text: I find them a place to stay. Clothes. Food. I don't ask if they're Irish or Jewish or Italian, or if they're worthy. I just help.

voice_notes: Man, mid-40s, Irish-New York accent, folksy, proud, chuckles at his own jokes.
text: And when Election Day comes, who do you think they vote for?

voice_notes: Man, mid-40s, Irish-New York accent, folksy, proud, chuckles at his own jokes.
text: Buying? Ha! It's friendship, young fella. Where's the government when a family is cold? Where are the reformers? They come once, make a speech, and go home.

voice_notes: Man, mid-40s, Irish-New York accent, folksy, proud, chuckles at his own jokes.
text: Tammany is there every day. Ask the families we helped last winter whether Tammany is bad.

voice_notes: Warm, measured adult narrator. 1880s newspaper editor reading a letter.
text: You write in your notebook: the machine helped people who needed it. But it also stole public money and expected votes in return.

voice_notes: Man, 40s, Norwegian accent, loud over noise, proud of the work.
text: Watch your head! Bricks coming up! You can't stand here without a reason, friend.

voice_notes: Man, 40s, Norwegian accent, loud over noise, proud of the work.
text: Land on this island costs a fortune! You can't build out, so you build up.

voice_notes: Man, 40s, Norwegian accent, loud over noise, proud of the work.
text: More floors, more offices, more rent. Simple.

voice_notes: Man, 40s, Norwegian accent, loud over noise, proud of the work.
text: Two inventions. First, the safe elevator. Mr. Otis made one that won't fall if the rope breaks. Who wants to climb ten floors of stairs?

voice_notes: Man, 40s, Norwegian accent, loud over noise, proud of the work.
text: Second, the frame. In Chicago, they put up the Home Insurance Building in 1885 with a metal skeleton inside. The frame holds up the building, not the walls.

voice_notes: Man, 40s, Norwegian accent, loud over noise, proud of the work.
text: People are starting to call them "sky-scrapers." Ha! Scraping the sky!

voice_notes: Man, 30s, Irish-New York accent, impatient and funny.
text: Horsecar up Broadway! Five cents! Step lively!

voice_notes: Man, 30s, Irish-New York accent, impatient and funny.
text: Horses pull the car on iron rails. Smoother than a carriage, and cheaper than a cab.

voice_notes: Man, 30s, Irish-New York accent, impatient and funny.
text: A clerk can live uptown and ride downtown to work. Twenty years ago, he'd have to live next to his office.

voice_notes: Man, 30s, Irish-New York accent, impatient and funny.
text: Cable cars, maybe! A steel cable under the street pulls the car. There's a line on Tenth Avenue since 1885. Out in San Francisco, they climb the hills!

voice_notes: Man, 30s, Irish-New York accent, impatient and funny.
text: And I hear Richmond, Virginia just started electric trolleys this year. Electric! No horses at all! Then what'll I do?

voice_notes: Man, 30s, gruff New Yorker, shouting over the trains.
text: Third Avenue El! Uptown trains! Steam engines on an iron road, right above the street!

voice_notes: Man, 30s, gruff New Yorker, shouting over the trains.
text: For Central Park? Ride to Fifty-Ninth Street and walk west. Or take the Sixth Avenue El, right to the Park's corner! Five cents!

voice_notes: Man, 30s, gruff New Yorker, shouting over the trains.
text: Noisy! Cinders and hot oil drip on your hat. Your windows go dark, and the whole building shakes every few minutes.

voice_notes: Man, 30s, gruff New Yorker, shouting over the trains.
text: Progress, they call it.

voice_notes: Man, 30s, gruff New Yorker, shouting over the trains.
text: All aboard! Hold onto your hat!

voice_notes: Man, 30s, Italian accent, out of breath, wry.
text: Hey, camera man! You want a picture? Take it quick. The foreman docks my pay if I stand still.

voice_notes: Man, 30s, Italian accent, out of breath, wry.
text: I carry bricks up the ladders, eleven stories, all day. No rope. No net. A dollar and a half.

voice_notes: Man, 30s, Italian accent, out of breath, wry.
text: Last month a man fell from the ninth floor. The next morning, another man had his job.

voice_notes: Young man, 18, New York accent, cheerful, rehearsed patter.
text: Going up! Mr. Otis's safety elevator, young fellow. If the rope breaks, the brakes catch us. Probably.

voice_notes: Young man, 18, New York accent, cheerful, rehearsed patter.
text: Eleven floors in under a minute. Nobody would rent an office up there if they had to climb.

voice_notes: Man, 50s, Scottish accent, strict but kind.
text: Welcome to Central Park! Kindly stay on the paths.

voice_notes: Man, 50s, Scottish accent, strict but kind.
text: Mr. Frederick Law Olmsted and Mr. Calvert Vaux designed it. They started back in 1858. Took twenty years.

voice_notes: Man, 50s, Scottish accent, strict but kind.
text: Mr. Olmsted said a city needs lungs. A place where rich and poor alike can breathe fresh air.

voice_notes: Man, 50s, Scottish accent, strict but kind.
text: Weekdays, mostly the carriages of the rich, out for a drive.

voice_notes: Man, 50s, Scottish accent, strict but kind.
text: Sundays, the working families come up from downtown. If they can spare the fare, and the time. Most work six days a week, you see.

voice_notes: Woman, 30s, Yiddish accent, practical and quick.
text: Photographer! Yes, it's us. Sunday is the only day we don't sew.

voice_notes: Woman, 30s, Yiddish accent, practical and quick.
text: Five cents each way, for each of us. So we come once a summer. But look how Sarah runs!

voice_notes: Girl, about 10, Yiddish accent, shy.
text: The grass is so green! We never see grass on Hester Street.

voice_notes: Girl, about 10, Yiddish accent, shy.
text: But the sign says we can't walk on it. Why make grass if you can't touch it?

voice_notes: Girl, about 16. Jewish, from near Kiev. Light Yiddish/Russian accent. Brave but tired.
text: Photographer! I hoped you would come.

voice_notes: Warm, measured adult narrator. 1880s newspaper editor reading a letter.
text: You hand Rivka the print you made on the ship. She stares at it for a long time.

voice_notes: Girl, about 16. Jewish, from near Kiev. Light Yiddish/Russian accent. Brave but tired.
text: That is us. That is really us. Shmuel, Mama, me.

voice_notes: Girl, about 16. Jewish, from near Kiev. Light Yiddish/Russian accent. Brave but tired.
text: Bubbe will hold this in her hands. She will see we are alive.

voice_notes: Warm, measured adult narrator. 1880s newspaper editor reading a letter.
text: She wipes her eyes with the back of her wrist and laughs at herself.

voice_notes: Girl, about 16. Jewish, from near Kiev. Light Yiddish/Russian accent. Brave but tired.
text: I work for Mr. Kessler now. Sleeves and buttonholes, eleven hours a day.

voice_notes: Girl, about 16. Jewish, from near Kiev. Light Yiddish/Russian accent. Brave but tired.
text: Two weeks, and he has not paid us. "Next Friday," he says. Every Friday is next Friday.

voice_notes: Girl, about 16. Jewish, from near Kiev. Light Yiddish/Russian accent. Brave but tired.
text: And we still owe the Kiever Society for the money that was stolen from us at Castle Garden. Every week, a little.

voice_notes: Girl, about 16. Jewish, from near Kiev. Light Yiddish/Russian accent. Brave but tired.
text: Esther, the girl on the box, says if we all sign the union card, Kessler must pay. Or we stop work, all together.

voice_notes: Girl, about 16. Jewish, from near Kiev. Light Yiddish/Russian accent. Brave but tired.
text: But if he finds out I signed, he throws me out. And Mama and Shmuel eat what I earn.

voice_notes: Girl, about 16. Jewish, from near Kiev. Light Yiddish/Russian accent. Brave but tired.
text: You have seen more of America than me. What should I do?

voice_notes: Girl, about 16. Jewish, from near Kiev. Light Yiddish/Russian accent. Brave but tired.
text: Yes. Yes! Papa used to say: one finger is easy to break. A fist is not.

voice_notes: Warm, measured adult narrator. 1880s newspaper editor reading a letter.
text: She signs in careful Yiddish letters, and then again in English: Rivka Abramowitz.

voice_notes: Girl, about 16. Jewish, from near Kiev. Light Yiddish/Russian accent. Brave but tired.
text: Maybe you are right. Maybe next season, when we have something saved.

voice_notes: Warm, measured adult narrator. 1880s newspaper editor reading a letter.
text: She folds the union card very small and slips it into her shoe.

voice_notes: Girl, about 16. Jewish, from near Kiev. Light Yiddish/Russian accent. Brave but tired.
text: Tomorrow is the election. Everyone on the street is shouting about it.

voice_notes: Girl, about 16. Jewish, from near Kiev. Light Yiddish/Russian accent. Brave but tired.
text: I cannot vote. Women cannot vote. Not Mama, not Mrs. Brennan, not anyone.

voice_notes: Girl, about 16. Jewish, from near Kiev. Light Yiddish/Russian accent. Brave but tired.
text: But I can shout. Maybe louder than the men.

voice_notes: Girl, about 16. Jewish, from near Kiev. Light Yiddish/Russian accent. Brave but tired.
text: If Kessler finds out, he finds out. I am not afraid. ...I am a little afraid.

voice_notes: Girl, about 16. Jewish, from near Kiev. Light Yiddish/Russian accent. Brave but tired.
text: The card is in my shoe. I can feel it when I walk.

voice_notes: Young woman, 19, Yiddish accent, fiery speaker, warm one-on-one.
text: Sisters! Brothers! Fourteen hours for three dollars a week! They tell us there is no money. There is money!

voice_notes: Young woman, 19, Yiddish accent, fiery speaker, warm one-on-one.
text: The United Hebrew Trades started just last month. Cloakmakers, bakers, typesetters.

voice_notes: Young woman, 19, Yiddish accent, fiery speaker, warm one-on-one.
text: Alone, they cheat us one by one. Together, they cannot!

voice_notes: Young woman, 19, Yiddish accent, fiery speaker, warm one-on-one.
text: Of course. The police broke up our meeting on Thursday.

voice_notes: Young woman, 19, Yiddish accent, fiery speaker, warm one-on-one.
text: But I am more afraid of my mother's hands. Thirty years of sewing. They don't open anymore.

voice_notes: Young woman, 19, Yiddish accent, fiery speaker, warm one-on-one.
text: We all stop work, on the same day. No coats, no money for the boss.

voice_notes: Young woman, 19, Yiddish accent, fiery speaker, warm one-on-one.
text: He can fire one girl. He cannot fire twenty. Not in November, with orders waiting.

voice_notes: Man, 40s, Yiddish-German accent, brusque and defensive, tired; not a cartoon villain.
text: You again, with the camera. You want to put me in your newspaper too?

voice_notes: Man, 40s, Yiddish-German accent, brusque and defensive, tired; not a cartoon villain.
text: Union, union. You know what the manufacturer told me? Cut prices ten percent, or he gives the contract to the next man.

voice_notes: Man, 40s, Yiddish-German accent, brusque and defensive, tired; not a cartoon villain.
text: So I hold the pay a little. I pay it! Eventually.

voice_notes: Man, 40s, Yiddish-German accent, brusque and defensive, tired; not a cartoon villain.
text: I came over in '72 with nothing. I sewed in a room like theirs for nine years. Now I am the boss, and everyone hates me.

voice_notes: Man, 40s, Yiddish-German accent, brusque and defensive, tired; not a cartoon villain.
text: This is America, kid. Somebody squeezes you, you squeeze somebody.

voice_notes: Man, 30s, Yiddish accent, kind, overworked, coughs a little.
text: So. You came back.

voice_notes: Man, 30s, Yiddish accent, kind, overworked, coughs a little.
text: Your picture was in every hand on Hester Street. My Sarah's face, at the machine.

voice_notes: Man, 30s, Yiddish accent, kind, overworked, coughs a little.
text: The next morning, Mr. Kessler came up those stairs and took the coats away. All of them. "Troublemakers," he said.

voice_notes: Warm, measured adult narrator. 1880s newspaper editor reading a letter.
text: The sewing machine is silent. Chana is washing other people's laundry in a tub.

voice_notes: Man, 30s, Yiddish accent, kind, overworked, coughs a little.
text: But. A lady from the Neighborhood Guild came, with your newspaper in her hand.

voice_notes: Man, 30s, Yiddish accent, kind, overworked, coughs a little.
text: Now Sarah goes to their class after school, instead of sewing buttons. She is learning to read English.

voice_notes: Man, 30s, Yiddish accent, kind, overworked, coughs a little.
text: So I don't know if I should thank you, or throw you down the stairs.

voice_notes: Man, 30s, Yiddish accent, kind, overworked, coughs a little.
text: You kept your word. Thank you.

voice_notes: Man, 30s, Yiddish accent, kind, overworked, coughs a little.
text: We still have Kessler's coats. Fourteen hours a day.

voice_notes: Man, 30s, Yiddish accent, kind, overworked, coughs a little.
text: Sarah still sews buttons. Nothing is worse. Nothing is better, either.

voice_notes: Man, 30s, Yiddish accent, kind, overworked, coughs a little.
text: Oh! A letter came for you. Here, at our address. It has a steamship company stamp.

voice_notes: Man, 30s, Yiddish accent, kind, overworked, coughs a little.
text: And tomorrow, I vote! Me!

voice_notes: Man, 30s, Yiddish accent, kind, overworked, coughs a little.
text: Mr. Quinn took me to the courthouse last month. I came in '82, six years, so it is legal. Twenty minutes, and I am a citizen, with papers.

voice_notes: Man, 30s, Yiddish accent, kind, overworked, coughs a little.
text: Quinn says, vote Grant. Mr. Whitcomb from the Guild says, vote Hewitt. Grant's people bring coal. Hewitt's people bring speeches.

voice_notes: Man, 30s, Yiddish accent, kind, overworked, coughs a little.
text: In Russia, the Tsar told me where I could live. Tomorrow, I help choose the mayor of New York. Can you believe it?

voice_notes: Woman, 40s, Yiddish accent, worried and gentle.
text: Rivka works so hard. I take in washing. And Shmuel goes to the public school!

voice_notes: Woman, 40s, Yiddish accent, worried and gentle.
text: He learns English faster than all of us. He corrects my English now. Like a little professor.

voice_notes: Boy, about 8.
text: Mr. Novak finished my horse! I tried to make it swim in the washtub. It sinks. But it's a very good horse.

voice_notes: Boy, about 8.
text: Mr. Novak gave Mama this horse for me. Then they put him back on the ship.

voice_notes: Boy, about 8.
text: Why did they send him back? He was nice. He wasn't a "public charge." He was Mr. Novak.

voice_notes: Man, 40s, Irish-New York accent, booming and friendly. Fictional Tammany ward boss.
text: Friends! Neighbors! Who brought coal when the blizzard came in March?

voice_notes: Man, 40s, Irish-New York accent, booming and friendly. Fictional Tammany ward boss.
text: Who found your cousin a job? Who stood next to your boy in front of the judge?

voice_notes: Man, 40s, Irish-New York accent, booming and friendly. Fictional Tammany ward boss.
text: Tomorrow, vote for Hugh J. Grant! The son of Irish immigrants! One of US!

voice_notes: Man, 40s, Irish-New York accent, booming and friendly. Fictional Tammany ward boss.
text: Hewitt! He wouldn't even review the St. Patrick's Day parade! Wouldn't fly the green flag over City Hall!

voice_notes: Man, 40s, Irish-New York accent, booming and friendly. Fictional Tammany ward boss.
text: He thinks we're dirt. He'll build parks for the rich and send inspectors to close your shops.

voice_notes: Man, 40s, Irish-New York accent, booming and friendly. Fictional Tammany ward boss.
text: Coal! Who needs coal? Grant's coal, free for the asking!

voice_notes: Woman, 50s, Irish accent, sharp-tongued, proud, defensive.
text: Tomorrow my Michael will be first in line at the polls. Women can't vote, more's the pity.

voice_notes: Woman, 50s, Irish accent, sharp-tongued, proud, defensive.
text: In March, Mayor Hewitt wouldn't review our parade on St. Patrick's Day. Wouldn't fly the green flag over City Hall.

voice_notes: Woman, 50s, Irish accent, sharp-tongued, proud, defensive.
text: As if we Irish hadn't built half this city with our backs.

voice_notes: Woman, 50s, Irish accent, sharp-tongued, proud, defensive.
text: Hugh Grant's father came over on the boats, like mine. That's Michael's vote.

voice_notes: Young man, 20s, educated American, earnest.
text: Leaflet? Vote for Mayor Hewitt! An honest man. Not one dollar stolen from the city.

voice_notes: Young man, 20s, educated American, earnest.
text: He passed the law for small parks in crowded neighborhoods, like this one. He wants a public railway under the streets.

voice_notes: Young man, 20s, educated American, earnest.
text: Tammany buys your vote with a sack of coal, then steals the coal money back from the city ten times over.

voice_notes: Young man, 20s, educated American, earnest.
text: ...He has said foolish things about the Irish. I admit that.

voice_notes: Young man, 20s, educated American, earnest.
text: But a mayor who insults you honestly is better than one who robs you kindly. Isn't he?

voice_notes: Man, 40s, Cantonese accent, calm, careful, a little guarded.
text: All of Mott Street talks about the election. Grant, Hewitt, Erhardt.

voice_notes: Man, 40s, Cantonese accent, calm, careful, a little guarded.
text: You want to know who I vote for?

voice_notes: Man, 40s, Cantonese accent, calm, careful, a little guarded.
text: The law says I will never vote. Not tomorrow. Not ever. I pay my taxes. I cannot choose.

voice_notes: Man, 40s, Cantonese accent, calm, careful, a little guarded.
text: And last month Congress passed the Scott Act. Now, if a Chinese worker goes home to visit his family, he can never come back.

voice_notes: Man, 40s, Cantonese accent, calm, careful, a little guarded.
text: My brother was saving to visit our mother. Now he will not go. He will not see her again.

voice_notes: Man, 20s, southern Italian accent, cheerful and proud, a little homesick.
text: Photographer! Look at me! Mr. Quinn found me work, on the new Times Building!

voice_notes: Man, 20s, southern Italian accent, cheerful and proud, a little homesick.
text: Eleven stories! I carry bricks up, up, up, all day. A dollar and a half, and no padrone taking his cut!

voice_notes: Man, 20s, southern Italian accent, cheerful and proud, a little homesick.
text: Quinn says I don't owe him anything. ...Except one little favor tomorrow. I tell you later.

voice_notes: Man, 20s, southern Italian accent, cheerful and proud, a little homesick.
text: Come see me on Park Row!

voice_notes: Boy, about 11, New York street accent, fast.
text: Extra, extra! Election tomorrow! Grant! Hewitt! Erhardt! Who'll be mayor? Read all about it, two cents!

voice_notes: Man, 20s, southern Italian accent, cheerful and proud, a little homesick.
text: You came! Look up. Eleven stories. Tonight my back will say hello to me.

voice_notes: Man, 20s, southern Italian accent, cheerful and proud, a little homesick.
text: Now. The favor. Mr. Quinn says tomorrow, I go to the polls and I say, "My name is Patrick Moran."

voice_notes: Man, 20s, southern Italian accent, cheerful and proud, a little homesick.
text: Patrick Moran died in August. But he is still on the voting list.

voice_notes: Man, 20s, southern Italian accent, cheerful and proud, a little homesick.
text: I am not a citizen. I cannot vote. But Quinn says, "Everybody does it. Do it, or the job goes to a fellow who will."

voice_notes: Man, 20s, southern Italian accent, cheerful and proud, a little homesick.
text: What do I do, photographer? No job, no money for Mamma.

voice_notes: Man, 20s, southern Italian accent, cheerful and proud, a little homesick.
text: You are right. My father always said: a man has his name and nothing else.

voice_notes: Man, 20s, southern Italian accent, cheerful and proud, a little homesick.
text: I keep my name. I tell Quinn tonight.

voice_notes: Warm, measured adult narrator. 1880s newspaper editor reading a letter.
text: He doesn't look proud. He looks scared.

voice_notes: Man, 20s, southern Italian accent, cheerful and proud, a little homesick.
text: Yes. Yes. One little vote. Who does it hurt?

voice_notes: Warm, measured adult narrator. 1880s newspaper editor reading a letter.
text: He laughs. But he doesn't look at you.

voice_notes: Man, 20s, southern Italian accent, cheerful and proud, a little homesick.
text: The newspapers? Then everyone knows it was me who talked...

voice_notes: Man, 20s, southern Italian accent, cheerful and proud, a little homesick.
text: ...But maybe they stop it. For everybody. All right. Tell your Mr. Haskins.

voice_notes: Man, 20s, southern Italian accent, cheerful and proud, a little homesick.
text: Now I climb, or the foreman docks me. Go up on the Potter Building roof next door, you can watch me work! Take my picture for Mamma!

voice_notes: Man, 20s, southern Italian accent, cheerful and proud, a little homesick.
text: Up on the Potter roof! Wave at me!

voice_notes: Man, 20s, southern Italian accent, cheerful and proud, a little homesick.
text: Fotografo! Up here! You see? I am higher than the church steeples!

voice_notes: Man, 20s, southern Italian accent, cheerful and proud, a little homesick.
text: Take my picture! For Mamma! Tell her I am a big man in America now!

voice_notes: Warm, measured adult narrator. 1880s newspaper editor reading a letter.
text: A board cracks, loud as a gunshot.

voice_notes: Warm, measured adult narrator. 1880s newspaper editor reading a letter.
text: Giuseppe drops through the open floor, bricks and all.

voice_notes: Warm, measured adult narrator. 1880s newspaper editor reading a letter.
text: He lands on the planking one story down. He doesn't move.

voice_notes: Warm, measured adult narrator. 1880s newspaper editor reading a letter.
text: ...Then he does. He is holding his arm and shouting in Italian. Alive.

voice_notes: Warm, measured adult narrator. 1880s newspaper editor reading a letter.
text: The men are lowering him down the ladders. Hurry down to the street.

voice_notes: Man, 20s, southern Italian accent, cheerful and proud, a little homesick.
text: Photographer... I am alive. The arm is broken. Maybe two ribs.

voice_notes: Man, 40s, Norwegian accent, loud over noise, proud of the work.
text: He can't carry a hod with one arm. No work, no pay. That's the rule. I don't make it.

voice_notes: Warm, measured adult narrator. 1880s newspaper editor reading a letter.
text: A crowd is gathering. No paper on Park Row has a picture of this yet. Your camera is in your hands.

voice_notes: Warm, measured adult narrator. 1880s newspaper editor reading a letter.
text: The shutter clicks. Giuseppe looks up into the lens, then away.

voice_notes: Man, 20s, southern Italian accent, cheerful and proud, a little homesick.
text: Even now, the camera? ...Go on. Maybe somebody should see.

voice_notes: Warm, measured adult narrator. 1880s newspaper editor reading a letter.
text: You set the camera on the paving stones and take his good hand. Across the street, a man from the World gets the picture instead.

voice_notes: Man, 20s, southern Italian accent, cheerful and proud, a little homesick.
text: Grazie. Stay a minute. Only a minute.

voice_notes: Man, 40s, Irish-New York accent, booming and friendly. Fictional Tammany ward boss.
text: Easy, easy, son! Tammany takes care of its own. I sent for Dr. Malone, and he's paid for.

voice_notes: Man, 40s, Irish-New York accent, booming and friendly. Fictional Tammany ward boss.
text: And Halvorsen, the job is his again when the arm heals. Isn't that right, Halvorsen?

voice_notes: Man, 40s, Norwegian accent, loud over noise, proud of the work.
text: ...If you say so, Mr. Quinn.

voice_notes: Man, 20s, southern Italian accent, cheerful and proud, a little homesick.
text: You see? Quinn is a good man. ...Right?

voice_notes: Man, 20s, southern Italian accent, cheerful and proud, a little homesick.
text: I told Quinn no, this morning. When I fell, I sent a boy to his club. He sent back a message: "Ask your new friends for help."

voice_notes: Man, 50s, southern Italian accent, calm, fatherly.
text: Coraggio, Giuseppe. The Società pays for the doctor. You paid your ten cents every week. Now we pay you.

voice_notes: Man, 20s, southern Italian accent, cheerful and proud, a little homesick.
text: Ten cents a week, and they did not forget me. My own people.

voice_notes: Man, 60s, American, dry humor, a bit cynical.
text: I've got it all, son. Repeaters, dead men on the voting lists, Quinn's name. It runs in tomorrow's paper.

voice_notes: Man, 50s, southern Italian accent, calm, fatherly.
text: And the Società will pay for the doctor. Coraggio, Giuseppe.

voice_notes: Man, 20s, southern Italian accent, cheerful and proud, a little homesick.
text: Tomorrow everyone knows I talked. Quinn will never give me work again.

voice_notes: Man, 20s, southern Italian accent, cheerful and proud, a little homesick.
text: But maybe no one else gets asked to be a dead man.

voice_notes: Same voice as the narrator: warm, measured, a little gruff in person.
text: There you are, kid. That plate of the man on the sidewalk: every paper on the Row wishes it had it.

voice_notes: Same voice as the narrator: warm, measured, a little gruff in person.
text: It will sell ten thousand copies. I hope he forgives you. I would not ask him.

voice_notes: Same voice as the narrator: warm, measured, a little gruff in person.
text: There you are, kid. The World has a picture of that fall and the Courier does not. I hear you were holding the man's hand.

voice_notes: Same voice as the narrator: warm, measured, a little gruff in person.
text: I hired a photographer. It seems I also hired a decent person. Do not tell the other editors.

voice_notes: Same voice as the narrator: warm, measured, a little gruff in person.
text: I've seen your plates. Good work. Hard work.

voice_notes: Same voice as the narrator: warm, measured, a little gruff in person.
text: Tomorrow, New York picks a mayor. The Courier has to say who it backs, and I want to hear it from someone who has walked those streets.

voice_notes: Same voice as the narrator: warm, measured, a little gruff in person.
text: Here is what each man stands for.

voice_notes: Same voice as the narrator: warm, measured, a little gruff in person.
text: So. Who does the Evening Courier endorse?

voice_notes: Same voice as the narrator: warm, measured, a little gruff in person.
text: Tammany's man. He'll feed the hungry, and the treasury will feed Tammany. Bold. All right, we print it.

voice_notes: Same voice as the narrator: warm, measured, a little gruff in person.
text: Honest Abe Hewitt. Clean and careful, and he can't stand half the people you photographed. All right, we print it.

voice_notes: Same voice as the narrator: warm, measured, a little gruff in person.
text: The Republican. Law and order. Hester Street will laugh at us, but all right, we print it.

voice_notes: Same voice as the narrator: warm, measured, a little gruff in person.
text: Go home and sleep. Tomorrow night, the whole city will be here on Park Row, waiting for the returns. Be here.

voice_notes: Same voice as the narrator: warm, measured, a little gruff in person.
text: Tomorrow night. Park Row. Be here.

voice_notes: Man, 30s, booming New York voice, theatrical.
text: RETURNS FROM THE FOURTH WARD! Grant, two thousand one hundred! Erhardt, eight hundred! Hewitt, six hundred!

voice_notes: Warm, measured adult narrator. 1880s newspaper editor reading a letter.
text: A roar goes up from the Tammany men. Someone throws a hat in the air. It doesn't come back.

voice_notes: Man, 30s, booming New York voice, theatrical.
text: SEVENTH WARD! Grant, three thousand! Hewitt, one thousand two hundred! Erhardt, nine hundred!

voice_notes: Warm, measured adult narrator. 1880s newspaper editor reading a letter.
text: A man in a silk hat shakes his head and lights a cigar.

voice_notes: Man, 30s, booming New York voice, theatrical.
text: WITH NEARLY ALL DISTRICTS REPORTING: Grant, one hundred fourteen thousand! Erhardt, seventy-three thousand! Hewitt, seventy-two thousand!

voice_notes: Man, 30s, booming New York voice, theatrical.
text: HUGH J. GRANT IS THE NEXT MAYOR OF NEW YORK!

voice_notes: Warm, measured adult narrator. 1880s newspaper editor reading a letter.
text: The square explodes. Tammany wins. Mayor Hewitt, the honest man, has finished third.

voice_notes: Man, 30s, booming New York voice, theatrical.
text: GRANT ELECTED! TAMMANY CARRIES THE CITY!

voice_notes: Girl, about 16. Jewish, from near Kiev. Light Yiddish/Russian accent. Brave but tired.
text: Kessler found my card on Wednesday. He threw me out in front of everyone.

voice_notes: Girl, about 16. Jewish, from near Kiev. Light Yiddish/Russian accent. Brave but tired.
text: So on Thursday, the whole shop walked out! All twenty of us! Esther says he will pay us everything by Monday. He has to. The orders are waiting.

voice_notes: Girl, about 16. Jewish, from near Kiev. Light Yiddish/Russian accent. Brave but tired.
text: I don't have a job. But I have nineteen sisters.

voice_notes: Girl, about 16. Jewish, from near Kiev. Light Yiddish/Russian accent. Brave but tired.
text: I still have my job. Kessler paid us half. Half!

voice_notes: Girl, about 16. Jewish, from near Kiev. Light Yiddish/Russian accent. Brave but tired.
text: Esther says next season every shop on the street will strike together. Next season, I sign.

voice_notes: Girl, about 16. Jewish, from near Kiev. Light Yiddish/Russian accent. Brave but tired.
text: Your newspaper backed Grant, and Grant won. I hope he remembers the girls who sew, not only the men who vote.

voice_notes: Girl, about 16. Jewish, from near Kiev. Light Yiddish/Russian accent. Brave but tired.
text: Your newspaper backed Hewitt. He lost. But you said what you believed. That is something.

voice_notes: Girl, about 16. Jewish, from near Kiev. Light Yiddish/Russian accent. Brave but tired.
text: Erhardt? Nobody on Hester Street even knows his face! You are a strange photographer.

voice_notes: Girl, about 16. Jewish, from near Kiev. Light Yiddish/Russian accent. Brave but tired.
text: Someday women will vote too. And I will be first in line. Before Mrs. Brennan.

voice_notes: Man, 20s, southern Italian accent, cheerful and proud, a little homesick.
text: I did it. I walked in, I said "Patrick Moran," they gave me the ballot. Nobody even looked at my face.

voice_notes: Man, 20s, southern Italian accent, cheerful and proud, a little homesick.
text: Quinn paid the doctor. I have my job when the arm heals. So why do I feel like I stole something?

voice_notes: Man, 20s, southern Italian accent, cheerful and proud, a little homesick.
text: No job, a broken arm, and Quinn's people look at me like a traitor.

voice_notes: Man, 20s, southern Italian accent, cheerful and proud, a little homesick.
text: But Patrick Moran can rest in peace. And so can I.

voice_notes: Man, 20s, southern Italian accent, cheerful and proud, a little homesick.
text: The Società says when the arm heals, there is work on the docks in Brooklyn. We will see.

voice_notes: Man, 20s, southern Italian accent, cheerful and proud, a little homesick.
text: Haskins's story is in this morning's Courier! Two of Quinn's repeaters were arrested at the polls today!

voice_notes: Man, 20s, southern Italian accent, cheerful and proud, a little homesick.
text: Quinn's men spat on my shoes. But this year, nobody voted as Patrick Moran.

voice_notes: Man, 20s, southern Italian accent, cheerful and proud, a little homesick.
text: You still carry my mother's lemon? ...Ha! It smells like nothing now. Keep it anyway.

voice_notes: Man, 20s, southern Italian accent, cheerful and proud, a little homesick.
text: Go, go. Write your story. Make me look rich.

voice_notes: Man, 30s, Yiddish accent, kind, overworked, coughs a little.
text: I voted! Me! Moishe Abramowitz, tailor, from a town the Tsar didn't want me in.

voice_notes: Man, 30s, Yiddish accent, kind, overworked, coughs a little.
text: I put a paper in a box, and they counted it. Like I count.

voice_notes: Man, 30s, Yiddish accent, kind, overworked, coughs a little.
text: Who did I pick? I won't tell you. A citizen has secrets now!

voice_notes: Man, 30s, Yiddish accent, kind, overworked, coughs a little.
text: And Sarah... the Guild teacher says she reads better than the big boys. Maybe your picture was worth it. Maybe.

voice_notes: Man, 30s, Yiddish accent, kind, overworked, coughs a little.
text: Sarah sewed four hundred buttons this week. She is asleep on her mother's shoulder.

voice_notes: Elderly man, 70s, Czech/Bohemian accent, quiet and dignified.
text: PHOTOGRAPHER! Here! Over here!

voice_notes: Warm, measured adult narrator. 1880s newspaper editor reading a letter.
text: Mr. Novak is holding the arm of a tall man with a red mustache, who is holding him back from the crowd.

voice_notes: Elderly man, 70s, Czech/Bohemian accent, quiet and dignified.
text: This is Tomas! My son! He came on the train from Chicago, two days and two nights!

voice_notes: Man, 40s, Czech-American accent, gentle, overwhelmed.
text: They told me a stranger paid for the telegram. Twenty-five cents. ...Thank you. I would never have known.

voice_notes: Elderly man, 70s, Czech/Bohemian accent, quiet and dignified.
text: Tomorrow, we go to Chicago. Tonight, I wanted to see an American election.

voice_notes: Elderly man, 70s, Czech/Bohemian accent, quiet and dignified.
text: So loud! Everybody shouts and nobody gets shot!

voice_notes: Woman, 50s, Irish accent, sharp-tongued, proud, defensive.
text: Grant won! Michael's dancing on a table in Clancy's saloon. One of our own, mayor of New York!

voice_notes: Woman, 50s, Irish accent, sharp-tongued, proud, defensive.
text: And your paper backed him. Maybe you're not so bad, for a newspaperman.

voice_notes: Woman, 50s, Irish accent, sharp-tongued, proud, defensive.
text: Your paper backed the other fellow. Well. You'll learn.

voice_notes: Young man, 20s, educated American, earnest.
text: Third. The honest man came third.

voice_notes: Young man, 20s, educated American, earnest.
text: Maybe we reformers talk too much and listen too little. Hester Street got coal from Tammany. From us, it got leaflets.

voice_notes: Man, 40s, Irish-New York accent, booming and friendly. Fictional Tammany ward boss.
text: Every ward! Every single one! Tell your readers: Tammany takes care of its own!

voice_notes: Man, 40s, Irish-New York accent, booming and friendly. Fictional Tammany ward boss.
text: And YOU. You and your Mr. Haskins cost me two good men today.

voice_notes: Man, 40s, Irish-New York accent, booming and friendly. Fictional Tammany ward boss.
text: ...I won't forget it, photographer. Tammany has a long memory.

voice_notes: Man, 40s, Irish-New York accent, booming and friendly. Fictional Tammany ward boss.
text: And your paper backed the winner! Drop by the club. There's always a cigar for a friend.

voice_notes: Man, 40s, Irish-New York accent, booming and friendly. Fictional Tammany ward boss.
text: Now if you'll excuse me, there's a parade to lead!

voice_notes: Man, 50s, American, brisk and official.
text: Your friends go on to the registry desk in the middle. Follow them, and keep out of my line.

voice_notes: Man, 30s, New York accent, tired, fast-talking but not unkind.
text: That old man from your ship is on the bench by the west wall. They are holding him. Go and see him, if you knew him.

voice_notes: Man, 30s, Yiddish accent, kind, overworked, coughs a little.
text: Mr. Riis, the newspaper man, is out in the yard with his camera. Talk to him. Then take your pictures, but think first.

voice_notes: Man, about 40, Danish accent, energetic, passionate about reform.
text: Go on. Photograph Chana and Sarah at their sewing, and the streets. Every plate you bring home is a witness.

voice_notes: Warm, measured adult narrator. 1880s newspaper editor reading a letter.
text:
Dear photographer,

I write this on the steamship. Tomorrow they send me back to Hamburg. No word came from Tomas. Maybe he moved. Maybe the clerk never sent my message.

Do not be sad for me. I saw America for two days. It was very loud.

I left the little horse with Mrs. Abramowitz, for Shmuel. Tell him it can swim.

Your friend,
Anton Novak

voice_notes: Warm, measured adult narrator. 1880s newspaper editor reading a letter.
text:
HUGH J. GRANT · Tammany Hall Democrat
Age 30, the son of Irish immigrants. Tammany's clubs give out coal, jobs, and help with citizenship papers. Critics say Tammany steals from the city and buys votes.

ABRAM S. HEWITT · Mayor, running for re-election (Citizens' ticket)
A wealthy, honest businessman. Pushed for small parks in crowded neighborhoods and a public subway. In March he refused to review the St. Patrick's Day parade, and many Irish and immigrant voters turned against him.

JOEL B. ERHARDT · Republican
A lawyer and former city police commissioner. Promises honest, businesslike government and strict law enforcement. Has little support on the Lower East Side.

voice_notes: Warm, measured adult narrator. 1880s newspaper editor reading a letter.
text:
Dear Cousin Rivka,

I am well, thank God. I live on Hester Street, New York, in two rooms with Chana and little Sarah. I sew coats. The work is hard, six days a week, but the pay is in dollars, and nobody burns your house.

I am sending money for three tickets. Bring Mama and Shmuel. When you come to Castle Garden, show them this address. Trust nobody outside the gate.

Your cousin,
Moishe

voice_notes: Warm, measured adult narrator. 1880s newspaper editor reading a letter.
text:
TO AMERICA!
FAST STEAMSHIPS TO NEW YORK
Safe. Quick. Only 10 to 14 days.
STEERAGE AT LOW FARES
Work for all! Land for all!
Ask our agent in your town.

voice_notes: Warm, measured adult narrator. 1880s newspaper editor reading a letter.
text:
Two-high wooden bunks fill the hold. Each has a straw mattress and a thin blanket. Suitcases and bundles are stuffed underneath. There is barely room to turn over.

Some passengers lie in their bunks all day, seasick. The air smells of sweat, salt, and coal smoke.

voice_notes: Warm, measured adult narrator. 1880s newspaper editor reading a letter.
text:
A big tin bucket of watery stew and a basket of hard black bread. A sailor bangs a spoon on the bucket: supper.

Passengers line up with their own tin cups and plates. A child looks into the bucket and starts to cry.

voice_notes: Warm, measured adult narrator. 1880s newspaper editor reading a letter.
text:
CASTLE GARDEN
LICENSED MONEY EXCHANGE
Fair rates posted daily.
Rubles. Lire. Marks. Pounds.
Do not change money with strangers outside the gate!

voice_notes: Warm, measured adult narrator. 1880s newspaper editor reading a letter.
text:
CHINESE STILL SHUT OUT

The Chinese Exclusion Act, passed by Congress in 1882, still bans Chinese laborers from entering the United States. Chinese people who are already here may not become citizens.

It is the first time the United States has shut out an entire group by nationality. Now Congress debates a new, stricter law: Chinese workers who visit their families in China would not be allowed back in.

voice_notes: Warm, measured adult narrator. 1880s newspaper editor reading a letter.
text:
Across the water, on Bedloe's Island, stands the Statue of Liberty, a gift from the people of France. It was dedicated in 1886, just two years ago.

Its copper skin is still reddish brown. Over the next twenty years, the weather will slowly turn it green. Its full name is "Liberty Enlightening the World," and at night its torch works as a lighthouse.

voice_notes: Warm, measured adult narrator. 1880s newspaper editor reading a letter.
text:
AMERICANS, WAKE UP!

Ships bring thousands of foreigners every week! They crowd our cities, take our jobs, and work for starvation wages. They do not speak our language or share our ways.

Support laws to keep them out! America for Americans!

voice_notes: Warm, measured adult narrator. 1880s newspaper editor reading a letter.
text:
KIEVER SOCIETY: For Members From Kiev and Nearby

Monthly dues: 25 cents.
Sick pay: $3 per week.
Loans to newcomers.
Burial in the society cemetery.
Meeting every Sunday, 2 o'clock.

(Notice written in Yiddish. You copy it into English.)

voice_notes: Warm, measured adult narrator. 1880s newspaper editor reading a letter.
text:
THE NEIGHBORHOOD GUILD
Founded 1886

Boys' and Girls' Clubs. Reading Room. Kindergarten. Classes in English. Lectures. Music.
All neighbors welcome.

voice_notes: Warm, measured adult narrator. 1880s newspaper editor reading a letter.
text:
A wooden shed at the back of the yard: the privy. It serves every family in the building, more than a hundred people.

Next to it, laundry flaps on lines strung between buildings. Children play beside the garbage barrels.

voice_notes: Warm, measured adult narrator. 1880s newspaper editor reading a letter.
text:
A cartoon by Thomas Nast, Harper's Weekly, August 19, 1871.

Boss Tweed and his friends stand in a circle. Each one points to the man next to him. The caption: "Who stole the people's money? Do tell. 'Twas him."

Nast's cartoons helped turn New Yorkers against the Tweed Ring.

voice_notes: Warm, measured adult narrator. 1880s newspaper editor reading a letter.
text:
The New York County Courthouse stands behind City Hall. It took about twenty years to build and cost the city around 13 million dollars, more than the United States paid for Alaska.

Much of that money went into the pockets of the Tweed Ring, through fake and padded bills.

voice_notes: Warm, measured adult narrator. 1880s newspaper editor reading a letter.
text:
In July 1871 The New York Times printed copies of the county's secret account books. They showed what friends of the Tweed Ring charged the city for this courthouse:

• Andrew J. Garvey, a plasterer: $133,187 for two days of work.
• A carpenter: $360,751 for one month, in a building with very little woodwork.
• Three tables and forty chairs: $179,729.

The contractors padded every bill, kept part of the extra, and paid the rest back to the Ring. Using public office to get rich like this is called graft.

Tweed was convicted in 1873 and died in the Ludlow Street Jail in 1878. Tammany Hall survived him.

voice_notes: Warm, measured adult narrator. 1880s newspaper editor reading a letter.
text:
Opened in 1883, the Brooklyn Bridge was the longest suspension bridge in the world. Its stone towers rise above every building in the city.

It connects New York to Brooklyn, which is still a separate city. Many of the workers who built it were immigrants. Some died building it.

voice_notes: Warm, measured adult narrator. 1880s newspaper editor reading a letter.
text:
FOR MAYOR
HUGH J. GRANT
Regular Democratic Nominee · Tammany Hall

Election Day: Tuesday, November 6, 1888.

Three men are running for mayor. Tammany Hall's clubs in every neighborhood are working to get out the vote for Grant.

voice_notes: Warm, measured adult narrator. 1880s newspaper editor reading a letter.
text:
TAMMANY HALL · DISTRICT CLUB

Men wanted for the city street crews. See Mr. Quinn.
Help with citizenship papers, Thursday evenings.
Free coal for families in need.
Grand picnic and boat ride for the children, tickets free.

VOTE THE STRAIGHT TICKET, NOVEMBER 6.

voice_notes: Warm, measured adult narrator. 1880s newspaper editor reading a letter.
text:
Eleven stories up, the whole city spreads out below. To the east, the towers of the Brooklyn Bridge. To the south, the harbor and the masts of ships. Only church steeples and a few new office buildings stand taller than you.

Next door, men are building the new Times Building even higher.

voice_notes: Warm, measured adult narrator. 1880s newspaper editor reading a letter.
text:
CENTRAL PARK: NOTICE

KEEP OFF THE GRASS.
No ball playing without permit.
No picnics upon the lawns.
No peddling.
Carriages to keep to the drives.

By order of the Park Commissioners.
